3. The case of the plaintiff, as made out in the plaint of the suit, was that the transferees sold the suit land for a consideration of Taka 4,500.00 to the defendants by registered safkabala deeds dated 21st Baishakh, 1382 BS corresponding to 5.5.75 and delivered khas possession of the suit land to the defendant petitioners. On the same date a deed of agreement was to have been executed by the defendants for retransfer of the said land on refund of the consideration money within 10 years but after 10 years of the execution of the said documents. The plaintiff demanded the execution of the retransfer deed from the defendants on ground of the consideration money but defendants having refused to execute the transfer deed the plaintiff was compelled to file the present suit for specific performance of contract. The defendant appeared in the said suit by filing written statement wherein they, inter alia, denied to have executed any deed of agreement in favour of the plaintiff and stated that they were not liable for re-transfer of the suit land to the plaintiff. They further stated that they had already transferred the suit land to their respective wives, defendants No. 3 and 4 on 8.12.1981. 

 7. Mr. Md. Lutfur Rahman Mazumder, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant respondent petitioners, has, inter alia, submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge acted illegally by making the alleged agreement as exhibit and received the same in evidence although the signatures of the petitioners in the agreement were not duly proved and the agreement was not registered as required under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It was further submitted that the petitioners had applied for examination of specimen signatures and thumb impression of the petitioners by an expert in the trial Court but they did not pursue the matter any further and, as such, the presumption that the alleged signatures were not genuine was 'irrefutable'. He further submitted that there was no discussion about any hand writing Expert. It was further argued that the agreement was signed on white paper and stamp paper and, therefore, the agreement was not valid in the eye of the law. 

 8. In support of his submission that the agreement for re-transfer must be registered he relied on section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. It provides that any transfer of a holding or of portion or share thereof either by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey or where the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and the transferee acquires the right to possess, and to enjoy the usufruct of such holding or portion or share shall, notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 7 years and the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 95 shall apply to such transfer. Section 95 provides that every such complete usufructurary mortgage shall be registered under the Registration Act 1908 (Act XVI of 1908). He has also referred to the case of Ali Ekabbar Farazi vs. Government of Bangladesh reported in 26 DLR 394. In that case it was inter alia, held: 

 9. It was therefore, argued by the learned advocate that without any stamp, and was therefore, no agreement for reconveyance under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as it was not registered. 

 10. Mr. Mihir Kanti Mazumder, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant opposite party, on the other hand, has submitted that the instant suit was filed for specific performance of contract and the plaintiff did not come for relief under section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for redemption of mortgage. Section 95A was inserted in the Act to protect the interest of transferor against an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey by treating it as usufructuary mortgage for 7 years, and special procedure for redemption of such mortgage. This Special Provision did not in any way take away the right of the transferor that he may have under any other law. In the instant case the plaintiff filed a suit for specific performance of contract reconvey the suit land. In the case of Shyamapada Singha and others vs. Dhlrendra Nath Bhadra alias Sutka Bhadra & others reported in 9 DLR 439 a Single Bench of the High Court, Dhaka observed: 

 13. The above mentioned decision, I think clearly stated law that an agreement for reconveyance could be specifically enforced and the provision for registration for such agreement as required under sub-section (2) of section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not applicable. Even an oral agreement if it could be proved by sufficient evidence may be specifically enforced by the transferee. It is, therefore, not correct to say that the agreement to reconvey the suit land in the instant case was required to be registered. 

 23. It is also argued by the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant petitioner that the appellate Court ought not to have relied on the evidence of PWs as the trial Court was in a better position to assess their evidence. In this connection he referred to a case of Dula Miah vs. Md. Ibrahim Khalil reported in 37 DLR 93 where a Single Bench of this Court held that the appellate Court should be very cautious about reversing the finding of facts by the trial Court. The appellate Court not having the opportunity of seeing and hearing any witness examined by the trial Court should be extremely careful in reversing the finding of fact by the trial Court. It is true that the appellate Court not having the benefit of examining the witness or seeing them should be extremely cautious to reverse the decision of question of facts but the appellate Court being the final court of determining questions of facts has the jurisdiction and responsibility to see that the evidence has been properly appreciated and assessed. In the instant case the appellate Court while reversing the judgment of the trial Court has discussed the evidence of all the 5 PWs and given cogent reasons for believing the evidence of the PW s. He has considered evidence of the plaintiff who gave evidence as PW 1. This PW 1 has given evidence of the two sale deeds executed in favour of the defendants and on the same day i.e. on 21st Baishakh, 1382 BS corresponding to 5.5.75 the defendant executed the agreement for reconveyance of the suit land after 5 years but within 10 years of the execution on refund of the consideration money of Taka 4000.00. This PW 1 also stated that because of his acquaintance with the defendant Abdul Kadir and his full trust in him he did not have the agreement registered. PW 2 Fazlur Rahman is a scribe. He deposed that he wrote out the agreement for reconveyance on the instruction of the plaintiff and the defendants although he said that he did not actually see the defendants executing the agreement He also said that he advised the parties to have the agreement registered but because of mutual trust of the parties in each other the agreement was not registered. He further stated in his cross examination that one Abdur Razzak was a witness to the agreements in whose presence the defendant signed and gave thumb impression on the agreement. PW 3 Abdul Jabbar was a witness to the agreement. He stated in his deposition that the defendant had executed the agreement in his presence. He also stated that witness Abdur Razak died. PW 4 Wazuddin was not very helpful in supporting the plaintiffs’ case. PW 5 Mitu Bepari stated that he had heard that the defendants had agreed to reconvey the land to the plaintiffs. After considering these oral evidence of the PW s and other evidence discussed the appellate Court found to his satisfaction that the plaintiff had proved that the agreement was executed by the defendants. The reason why the appellate Court disbelieved the evidence of the PWs and other evidence discussed the appellate Court found to his satisfaction that the plaintiff had proved that the agreement was executed by the defendants. The reason why the appellate Court disbelieved the evidence of the DWs was because DW 1 had denied having signed the Vokalatnama or having put thumb impression, but the appellate Court found that these two defendants Abdul Kadir and Saizuddin on 15.5.84 had put their thumb impression and signature on Vokalatnama filed first before the 6th Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka being the present case and, therefore, the contention that the defendant No. 1 could not write was proved to be false. It is in these circumstances that the appellate Court found that defendant's evidence not trustworthy or which could be relied on. The appellate Court being the final Court of question of fact this court in its revisional jurisdiction would not go into the question to see if the appellate Court correctly reassessed the evidence in reversing the finding of fact by the trial Court.
